title: "Uncertainty in a fitted slope"

  enabled: true

The fitted Provo regression slope is one estimate. **Regression uncertainty** describes how that estimator would vary under a repeated-sampling model.

## Conventional OLS uncertainty

Write the linear model in matrix form:

$$
\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2\mathbf I).
$$

The OLS estimator is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf Y.
$$

Because a linear transformation of a normal vector is normal,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X]
=
\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}.
$$

Replacing $\sigma^2$ with

$$
s^2=\frac{\sum_i e_i^2}{n-p}
$$

gives the conventional covariance estimate. Here $p$ is the number of fitted coefficients, including the intercept.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-regression-uncertainty
library(ggplot2)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)

fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
X <- model.matrix(fit)
s_squared <- sum(residuals(fit)^2) / df.residual(fit)
covariance_by_hand <- s_squared * solve(crossprod(X))
conventional_se <- sqrt(diag(covariance_by_hand))

cluster_covariance <- vcovCL(
  fit,
  cluster = provo$Text_ID,
  type = "HC1"
)
cluster_se <- sqrt(diag(cluster_covariance))

stopifnot(
  max(abs(covariance_by_hand - vcov(fit))) < 1e-12,
  length(unique(provo$Text_ID)) == 55L
)

data.frame(
  term = names(coef(fit)),
  estimate = coef(fit),
  conventional_se = conventional_se,
  passage_clustered_se = cluster_se
)
```

The conventional slope standard error is `r sprintf("%.6f", conventional_se[["cloze_surprisal_c"]])`; the passage-clustered HC1 sensitivity estimate is `r sprintf("%.6f", cluster_se[["cloze_surprisal_c"]])`. The latter allows arbitrary residual dependence within the observed passages while treating passages as independent clusters.

This sensitivity calculation does not recover reader variation. The raw readers were removed by aggregation, so neither uncertainty estimate substitutes for a participant-by-item model.

## Mean and response uncertainty

At predictor row $\mathbf x_0$, uncertainty in the fitted conditional mean is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\mu_0)
=
s^2\mathbf x_0^\top(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf x_0.
$$

A new response includes additional observation variance:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(Y_0-\widehat\mu_0)
=
s^2\left\{1+\mathbf x_0^\top(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf x_0\right\}.
$$

Thus a prediction interval is wider than a confidence interval for the mean.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-regression-uncertainty
#| fig-cap: "Provo positions, the OLS mean, its confidence band, and the wider response prediction limits."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
mean_interval <- predict(fit, newdata = grid, interval = "confidence")
response_interval <- predict(fit, newdata = grid, interval = "prediction")
grid$fit <- mean_interval[, "fit"]
grid$mean_low <- mean_interval[, "lwr"]
grid$mean_high <- mean_interval[, "upr"]
grid$response_low <- response_interval[, "lwr"]
grid$response_high <- response_interval[, "upr"]

point_opacity <- 0.2
interval_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = grid,
    aes(x = cloze_surprisal_bits, ymin = response_low, ymax = response_high),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "grey85"
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = grid,
    aes(x = cloze_surprisal_bits, ymin = mean_low, ymax = mean_high),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#2C6E9B",
    alpha = interval_opacity
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fit),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first-fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Check your understanding

1. Which assumption yields the factor $\sigma^2\mathbf I$?
2. Why does the response prediction variance contain an extra $1$?
3. Which grouping unit does the clustered sensitivity analysis retain?
4. Why can it not represent reader-level uncertainty?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Independent, homoscedastic errors with common variance $\sigma^2$ yield $\operatorname{Var}[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X]=\sigma^2\mathbf I$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A new response contains both uncertainty in the fitted mean and a new observation error with variance $\sigma^2$, represented by the extra $1$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The passage-clustered HC1 sensitivity analysis retains the Provo passage as the clustering unit through `Text_ID`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The item-position table has already aggregated away reader identities and trial-level responses, so reader covariance cannot be estimated. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](coefficient-of-determination.qmd) measures the reduction in squared error relative to a mean-only baseline.
